title: Meetings with the Labour Minister and the Textile Minister
author: Editorial Desk
summary: A BMS delegation raised workers' issues on 1 September 2026.
body:
On **1 September 2026**, a high-level delegation of BMS held two ministerial meetings, one on the Labour Codes and one on the textile industry. These came a fortnight after the nationwide Demands Day of 17 August. This post sets out what BMS has reported about each meeting, what was not reported, and how readers can judge the results.

## Context: protest, then dialogue

BMS's Ranchi working committee in late July 2026 decided on the 17 August programme. On that day, units held dharnas and demonstrations and submitted memoranda to the Prime Minister, the Finance Minister and the Labour Minister through district authorities, and a Delhi delegation met the Labour Secretary. Two weeks later came direct meetings with ministers. That sequence is not accidental; it follows BMS's stated method of responsive cooperation, which uses pressure from the ground to open a conversation and then continues the conversation at the top.

## The Labour Minister

The delegation met **Dr Mansukh Mandaviya**, the Union Minister for Labour and Employment, and raised **anti-worker provisions in the new Labour Codes**, as reported on the BMS website. The headline of BMS's report says the Government gave an assurance of early amendments. The page is in Hindi, gives no list of attendees and does not say which provisions would be amended or when, and the exact date of the meeting is not stated in the text. Those limits matter: an assurance of early amendment is a statement of intent and is not yet a change in the law.

To understand what was at stake, recall BMS's position. At its Ranchi meeting it recorded objections on 13 points in the Industrial Relations Code, such as definitions and recognition of negotiating unions, and on 15 provisions of the OSH Code, such as the definitions of "factory" and "work activity". Amendments to the Codes themselves need Parliament, while many details, such as thresholds and procedures, can be altered by rules framed by the Centre and the States. The Minister had also earlier told a BMS delegation of 15 federations, in a report published in November 2025, that the Government was committed to extending social security coverage to all unorganised-sector workers and treats it as a top priority.

## The Textile Minister

A delegation also met the **Union Textile Minister, Shri Giriraj Singh**, for about 75 minutes, according to BMS's note, which was published on 3 September. It was led by B. Surendran, All India Organising Secretary, with Anil Dhumne, All India Vice President, Jai Nath Choubey, textile sector in-charge, Shyam Singh Chouhan of the Vastra Udyog federation, Harishankar Prasad of the Jute federation and Ghanashyam Pandey of the textile federation.

The issues raised were these.

- **National Textile Corporation mills.** Pending wage payments, alleged victimisation of union leaders in Coimbatore, restarting production in 12 modernised mills, and a special package.
- **Jute.** A special team to study labour colony quarters in West Bengal, incentives for product diversification, an end to what BMS called exploitation by private management, wage increases, regularisation of contract labour and support for jute farmers.
- **Handloom and silk.** Priority for these labour-intensive sectors, skill training in modern technology and designs, market access and common handloom clusters acting as single-window platforms.
- **Readymade garments.** Mega textile parks in selected clusters across States.
- **Wage board.** A board to negotiate wage structures, because wages fixed only on the Consumer Price Index were called unjust. The delegation cited a floor-level worker in Bhilwara earning Rs 470 a day.

According to BMS, the Minister responded positively. It reports that he asked officials to form a special team to study the labour colonies of jute mills, agreed on measures to raise the incomes of handloom, powerloom, silk and garment workers, said the Government was exploring all possible ways to settle NTC wage dues, and aimed to increase jute production on 1.5 lakh acres, which would expand employment. It adds that special plans under PM MITRA would be formulated to create more livelihoods in garments, and that he advised the delegation to consider alternative fibres to meet changing needs.

## What the report does not say

BMS's note does not report any response on the wage board, on the Coimbatore allegations, on restarting the 12 mills or on the special NTC package. It is also BMS's own account of the meeting, not an independent record. A fair reading is that the meeting produced some concrete commitments, such as the study team, and left several of the larger demands open. The Ministry of Textiles and the Press Information Bureau are the places to look for any official record of follow-up.

## Why such meetings matter

- They place **written demands** before the decision-maker.
- They allow follow-up by the ministry and the union, since there is now a named person and a date.
- They keep the debate on the Codes **inside a tripartite process** rather than only on the street.
- They give federations a chance to raise sector problems that do not get attention in general campaigns, as jute and handloom did here.

BMS has used the same approach before. A BMS delegation met the Home Minister in June 2025 on NTC mills and was told, according to BMS, that he would speak to the concerned minister about salary dues and study the proposal to restart 12 mills. Another delegation met the Education Minister in 2025 on mid-day meal workers' honoraria. Such earlier examples allow members to see how far promises were converted into results, and in the NTC case the 2026 meeting shows that the same issues were still being pressed more than a year later.

## Measuring the result

A meeting is a first step. The results are seen in changes to rules, notifications, budgets and schemes. The question for members is what is done in the next six months. Five signs are worth tracking:

1. Whether the Labour Ministry publishes proposed amendments to the Industrial Relations Code or the OSH Code, or draft rules that address BMS's points.
2. Whether the special team on jute labour colonies is constituted and visits them.
3. Whether NTC wage dues are paid, and whether any of the 12 mills restart.
4. Whether PM MITRA or other schemes include conditions on wages for garment workers.
5. Whether a wage board for textile workers is considered.

## BMS's pattern

Programme of action on the ground, such as the 17 August demonstrations, followed by a meeting with ministers: this is the standard BMS rhythm. It is neither the confrontation of an all-out strike nor the quiet of a private representation. Its strength is that it keeps both routes open, and its test, as for every union, is whether members can point to something that changed in their workplace.
